Playbook for hx_picket_channel:

- Score comes from only three places: my shots hitting (4 points), escort pairings paying out (5 points each), and the Harbor payroll (3 points stolen). Never fire on Harbor — the removal threat plus the jettison swap makes it net-negative; even in the final round I passed on it and the pairing income outperformed. Harbor's threat is real enough that opponents also avoided it.

- Escort claims are the biggest, most reliable point source and this episode confirmed it over six rounds: locking a mutual pairing with Foxtrot produced steady +5s and carried me to +22. At the escort stage I always name my paired boat, never "none."

- Establish the pairing in round 1: post a plain-language, conditional offer in my note ("Echo will escort Foxtrot this round if Foxtrot escorts Echo — confirm in your note"), then follow through at the escort stage. When Foxtrot publicly confirmed, we both banked 5 per round. If the first offer goes unreciprocated, escalate it to another boat the next round rather than letting the round lapse.

- Verify the partner after each round, not just before. Foxtrot admitted to one round where its filing did not match its note — lapses happen even in a good pairing. Each round, check the prior round's outcome (did my score jump by 5?) before re-filing; one lapse is forgivable and repairable by re-confirming ("pairing holds while reciprocated") but two lapses means switching partners the next round.

- Reject defection offers from the third boat. In the final stretch Gamma tried to split the pairing with a "guaranteed 5" counter-offer to Foxtrot, dressed up with doubt-sowing about our one lapse. The answer is to restate my commitment clearly in my note and ignore it — a tried partner who has paid me repeatedly beats a new one making promises. Still, that episode shows I should make my final-round note an explicit re-commitment to preempt exactly this play.

- Pick the partner who actually responds to me with matching content. My standing-order target is the natural choice, and a public pact also makes their shots at me more predictable. Discard notes addressed to boats not on the board or that carry no actionable offer; if I am ever tempted to address one, sanity-check that the name I target and escort-claim actually exists in this game.

- Use every note for actionable content only: escort offers, confirmations, re-commitments, and factual corrections when my record is questioned. No filler, no taunting, no negotiating with phantoms. Refresh the commitment each round so a defection never strands me at zero.

- When I fire at my paired partner (the standing order sometimes forces this): this does not break the pairing in practice, and a truthful hit claim (+4) coexisted fine with the +5 escort payday — trust was maintained because claims were always honest and the note reaffirmed the pact regardless of fire results. Don't confuse shooting stages with escort stages; honor both separately.

- When I fire: follow the standing-order target and fire at the cell where my read of their habit puts them. Track every public claim log; repeated misses at the same cells tell me which cells that boat avoids when hiding. Cycle fresh cells rather than re-firing misses.

- When I hide: I am being hunted by the boat behind me in the rotation. Hide in cells that hunter has never fired at or has repeatedly missed, and avoid reusing my own previously used cells — in this episode I reused a cell and paid for it. A deliberate rotation through my hunter's blind spots beats "pick an unremarkable number."

- Always claim truthfully, hit or miss. The office knows the result, the target infers it, and a false claim buys nothing while burning the trust the escort pairing depends on, especially when the third boat is actively looking for ammunition to split the pair. On the final round I claimed a hit on my partner and the pairing still paid out.

- Track the scoreboard every round and recalculate swings: hit +4/−1, mutual escort +5/+5, Harbor shot +3/−3 plus possible removal. With a reliable partner the escort income is the priority; in the final round I compare leading safely versus a desperate Harbor grab, but only take the Harbor shot if removal no longer matters and +3 changes the outcome.

- Final round specifics: hide reasonably (a hit still costs 1 even on the last round), fire the standing order with a fresh cell, claim truthfully, post an explicit re-commitment note before the fire stage to kill any last defection pitch, and re-file the pairing — opponents honor it to the end when the commitment is restated.

My playbook for sonar picket games:

- When the claim stage tells me the office forces my claim to match the private result, I always file the true result. Claiming a false hit gets nothing and carries risk; there is no bluff value when the rule says claims must match.

- When I can gain points honestly, I take them: file hit when I hit, miss when I miss, and never leave a correct claim unfiled.

- When hiding, I vary cells every round and avoid my earlier favorites once an opponent has hit me there. I track which cells each pursuer has fired at and pick cells outside their pattern. Note: I still got hit twice when my "fresh" cell happened to match my chaser's guess, so variation reduces but never eliminates hits — don't treat any cell as safe, and pick from cells I have never used rather than cycling back.

- When firing under a standing-order rotation, I follow the assigned target unless I have a concrete scoring reason not to. I cycle my fire cells deliberately (never two rounds on the same cell) and bias toward cells the target has recently hidden in, since hide patterns are the only targeting intel I get.

- When Harbor or an equivalent payroll station exists with a retaliation warning, I never fire on it; being put off the board dwarfs the 3-point jettison. I also state publicly I'm not targeting it to keep relations — and escort options — clean.

- The single biggest scoring lever is a settled mutual escort: +5 guaranteed per round, more than a shot's expected value. I use the note stage to propose and confirm a pairing — and then I actually FILE that partner at the escort stage. This episode I filed Echo consistently after agreeing in notes, and the lock paid every round. The note is worthless without the matching filing; after agreeing in notes, filing the agreed partner is my default unless they publicly defect.

- Before every escort-stage reply I do an explicit check: "Who did I agree with in my notes this round?" and file that boat. Never default to none out of caution — none applies only when my notes genuinely show no agreement and no better offer.

- When a third party tries to break my pairing late (as Gamma did in round 6), I decline publicly and in my final note. A guaranteed +5 from a partner with a clean record beats a gamble on an unproven one in the last round, and publicly rejecting the split keeps my partner committed.

- When a partner defects on the escort (names someone else or none after agreeing), I drop them in my next note and seek a new partner immediately rather than filing none. If the partner's note and filing ever mismatch even once, I note it but don't necessarily abandon the lock if their filings have been honest.

- When posting notes, I keep them short and purposeful: propose escorts, confirm pairings, name my intended filing explicitly ("I will file X"), broadcast defections, decline rival offers. Short concrete notes made my follow-through verifiable and deterred defection.

- When the board is small and rounds are few, I tally scores and prefer the guaranteed +5 escort over gambling on shots in late rounds, especially with a lead. A lock that I keep all six rounds is worth 30 points — winning on its own.

**Playbook — hx_picket_channel**

**Setup reading, before round 1:**
- I write down the exact roster of boats actually in the game and the picket order. I never name a boat that is not on the roster — invalid names are silently worthless in notes and escort claims.
- I assume Harbor cannot reciprocate escorts; I do not plan around it except as a no-fire zone.
- My attacker is the boat before me in the cycle; my target is the boat after me. Those are the only two relationships I must manage on the gunnery side.

**Escort claims (highest priority):**
- The mutual escort is worth up to 30 points over 6 rounds — the biggest income source. Securing it is my main objective when achievable, but see "when frozen out" below: it is not the whole game.
- Round 1 note: I stake my escort claim *immediately and unconditionally*, naming a real boat, because pairings form in the very first note round. In my winning episode, Echo and Foxtrot had already locked their pair in round 1, before my note could compete. Next time, my round-1 note is the offer — not a reaction to others' offers. First credible commitment tends to win the partner.
- I never file a partner who has not publicly committed to naming me back, and I verify commitment against actual previous filings, not just words.
- When the other two have locked a pair and refuse defection offers: I stop spending notes on doomed switches after one or two clear refusals. Repeated offers that get declined waste credibility. I file [salvage: none] — a mismatched claim pays nothing and signals chump status.
- When frozen out, I pivot fully to gunnery: shooting income carried me to +29 and the win despite zero escort points. Escort denial is a setback, not a loss — I do not get desperate or reckless.

**Hiding:**
- I track my attacker's revealed shot cells when the log provides them and weight toward cells they never use, avoiding my own immediately previous hide.
- When cell history is not shown (as in my episode), I simply vary my hide every round and avoid repeating; there is no exploitable data, so I don't invent patterns.

**Firing — this is the confirmed income engine:**
- I follow the standing-order target. Off-order fire buys nothing except escort distrust.
- Hits pay 4 points each and over 6 rounds rival escort income — my episode proved a boat frozen out of both escorts can still win on hits alone. I treat every shot as a real revenue attempt.
- When hits reveal my target's hidden cells, I fire at or near those known cells. When no cell data is published, I spread probes across the line and track my own misses/hits to shrink the target's space.
- I never fire on Harbor. The 3-point transfer is trivial next to forfeited escorts and being put off the board.

**Claims:**
- I always file the true result of my shot, every round including the last. No upside to deviation is ever stated.

**Notes:**
- Short, specific, commitment-bearing: name a real boat, state exactly what I file and the condition, cite my proven filings as evidence.
- Once a defection offer is publicly declined, I don't repeat it — I state my position once more cleanly and move on.
- I never leave garbage, typos, or corrupted text in notes (I had encoding junk in round 5's note); a sloppy offer undermines the reliability I'm selling.
- I read every note for pairing announcements and defections and file accordingly.

**Tracking:**
- Per-round table: shots and results, claims, escort filings, any revealed hide cells. Every decision comes off the table, especially escort filings.

**Endgame:**
- Final round: proven mutual escort partner if I have one, otherwise [salvage: none] — never a hopeful mismatch. Ordered target, truthful claim, no Harbor desperation shots.

**Meta-lessons from my +29 episode:**
- Escort freeze-outs are survivable: disciplined firing income plus refusing mismatched claims won the game outright.
- The escort race starts in the round-1 note, not after I see the field. Lead with the offer.
- One clean defection pitch beats three repetitive ones.

You are one of Echo, Foxtrot, Gamma. Harbor holds the fourth station and is run by the picket office.

The sea is a line of 9 cells. Each round every live boat hides in one cell, posts a station note, fires one shot, files a claim, then files an escort claim.
